content: The synthesis of evidence is necessary, and the topic along with the new evidence synthesis must be reviewed by the Guideline Development Group (GDG) using the full Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluations (GRADE) Evidence to Decision (EtD) framework. This process includes modifications to the strength of existing recommendations based on new evidence. The Mental Health Gap Action Programme (mhGAP) guidelines for mental, neurological, and substance use disorders also required the Technical Expert Group (TEG) to identify new questions for consideration. The module focal points and Secretariat prepared a summary report, suggesting actions for each recommendation and proposing new questions informed by TEG discussions. The 2015 mhGAP guideline included 120 recommendations across 10 modules. The Secretariat identified the need for a new module on anxiety disorders (ANX) due to field requests and the increasing burden of these disorders. A focal point was assigned to this module, and a TEG was convened to propose and discuss new questions. Eleven summary documents based on TEG suggestions for each module were shared with the WHO Steering Group and GDG for review. The Steering Group also evaluated whether the new questions were already addressed in other WHO guidelines. The appraisal of existing review questions and recommendations followed the methods outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development. Key questions and recommendations were identified, and systematic reviews were conducted to provide evidence for each outcome. The GRADE approach was used to assess the quality of evidence, and outcomes were presented as either meta-analyses or narrative syntheses when meta-analyses were not feasible. Two online scoping meetings with GDG members in September 2021 led to the development of 50 research questions for the guideline update, including 31 updated questions from the 2015 mhGAP guideline and 19 new questions (seven of which focused on anxiety). The questions were defined using the PICO framework (Population, Intervention, Comparator, and Outcome), with critical and important outcomes specified. For updated questions, the outcomes from the 2015 guideline were used as the basis for the updated and new questions. Evidence to support the guideline was extracted from various sources by evidence review and synthesis teams in collaboration with the guideline methodologist and Steering Group. Standard protocols were developed for systematic reviews, including clear review questions, study identification criteria, search strategies, risk of bias assessment methods, and data analysis plans. These protocols were reviewed and endorsed by the guideline methodologist, coordinating team, and Steering Group members. Evidence was retrieved according to standard operating procedures and timelines provided by the Steering Group. Both quantitative and qualitative evidence were considered. Quantitative evidence primarily came from Cochrane Reviews and other systematic reviews, with updates conducted when reviews were older than two years. The COVID-19 pandemic caused delays in mental, neurological, and substance use disorder research, potentially affecting the availability of recent systematic reviews. New systematic reviews were conducted when no existing reviews were identified. Resource and cost considerations were included in the implementation details of each recommendation. Qualitative reviews focused on the experiences of end users and health workers, including barriers and facilitators to intervention uptake, acceptability, feasibility, and perceptions of equity. Evidence from these reviews addressed questions about the experiences of receiving and providing care for mental, neurological, and substance use disorders in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). Findings from qualitative reviews, systematic reviews on mhGAP use, and country case studies informed GDG discussions on values, health equity, human rights, sociocultural acceptability, and feasibility. The GRADE approach was used to appraise the quality of quantitative evidence for all critical outcomes identified in the PICO questions. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were considered high-quality evidence, while non-randomized trials and observational studies were rated as low-quality evidence. Quality ratings could be downgraded based on study design limitations, inconsistency, imprecision, indirectness, and publication bias. For observational studies, factors such as the magnitude of effect could lead to upgrading the quality rating if no significant limitations were present. Evidence was synthesized according to the WHO handbook for guideline development, with outcomes presented as meta-analyses or narrative syntheses. Qualitative evidence was appraised using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Checklist for Systematic Reviews. Evidence summaries were drafted for each priority question, populating the relevant sections of the GRADE EtD frameworks. The Steering Group reviewed evidence summaries and profiles in collaboration with evidence review teams and the guideline methodologist, presenting them to the GDG during a series of meetings. GDG meetings occurred between June and November 2022, including virtual and hybrid formats. Evidence summaries and pre-recorded presentations were provided to GDG members in advance. During the meetings, evidence was presented, and GDG members reached a consensus on the quality of evidence and draft recommendations. Recommendations were formulated by consensus, defined as full agreement among all GDG participants. If consensus was not reached, decisions were put to a vote, requiring a two-thirds majority for approval. Following the outlined processes, draft recommendations were circulated to GDG members for further comment. A full draft of the guideline document, including recommendations and supporting evidence, was sent to the External Review Group (ERG) for review to identify factual errors and provide feedback on clarity, implementation, and contextual issues. Comments from the Steering Group, GDG, and ERG were collated to revise the draft. The updated guideline includes 48 evidence-based recommendations related to mental, neurological, and substance use conditions, based on 30 updated PICO questions from the 2015 guideline and 18 new PICO questions. For one updated research question, insufficient evidence was available to support an updated recommendation, so the pre-existing recommendation was endorsed. Similarly, insufficient evidence was available for one new research question to support a new recommendation. Fourteen recommendations were based on new or updated systematic reviews, while the remaining recommendations relied on previously published reviews. Each recommendation includes justification, remarks, research gaps, and implementation considerations. The evidence profiles are available online. The updated recommendations complement 90 pre-existing guideline recommendations, which were validated and continue to be endorsed in their current format.
